period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

section_titles: Line of symmetry and mirror line
periods.activity_title: Fold, Press, Fly — Meeting the Mirror Line

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 1. Ink Design, p.164
tasks_in_class.description: Fold a sheet of paper in half, sprinkle water-colour drops at the fold, press to spread colour, open and observe the symmetrical ink design produced.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (a)–(c), p.165
tasks_in_class.description: Mark the line of symmetry in Fig. 3, 4, and 5; count how many lines of symmetry Fig. 8 has; decide where to place a mirror to see the right-half reflection and whether it matches the left half.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (d)–(h), p.165
tasks_in_class.description: Fly the symmetrical plane; try making an asymmetrical plane; fly both and observe which flies longer; share observations with friends.

time_bands.activity: Distribute square sheets and water-colours. Students fold paper in half, drop paint near the fold, press firmly, and unfold to reveal their ink design — Let Us Do, 1. Ink Design, p.164 ("fold, sprinkle colour, press, open and observe...."). Pairs compare designs and describe what they notice about the two halves.

Students fold and assemble the paper airplane following the textbook diagrams. At each fold stage they mark the line of symmetry on Fig. 3, 4, and 5; count lines of symmetry on Fig. 8; and use a small hand-mirror to check whether the right-half reflection matches the left — Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (a)–(c), p.165 ("mark the line of symmetry in Fig. 3, 4, and 5...."). The teacher names the fold line a 'mirror line' and writes both terms on the board.

Students fly their symmetric planes, then fold an asymmetric version and fly it — Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (d)–(h), p.165 ("fly symmetrical plane; make asymmetric plane; fly both...."). Small groups share observations about flight distance. A brief whole-class round collects one observation from each group.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have worked with rangoli symmetry and mask-making in Grade 3 will connect the ink-blot fold naturally to the idea of mirror halves — naming that prior experience grounds the new vocabulary of 'mirror line.' A common error is assuming that any fold line on the airplane is a line of symmetry; prompt students to check that both halves match exactly by placing the mirror along each proposed line.

section_titles: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
periods.activity_title: Predict Before You Cut — Fold-and-Cut Challenges

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, p.166
tasks_in_class.description: Take a square sheet of paper; fold and cut to reproduce Mini's design (fold twice, straight corner cut + two side squares removed).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 1, p.166
tasks_in_class.description: Predict where the hole and cut will appear when Rani's twice-folded paper (corner cut + two side squares) is opened.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 3, p.166
tasks_in_class.description: Fold a paper twice. Where would you cut to make a square hole in the centre? How many cuts are required?

homework.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 2, p.166
homework.description: Fold a piece of paper once; put two cuts in the middle as shown. How many sides will the shape have when you open the folded paper?

time_bands.activity: Each student takes a square sheet, folds it twice, makes Mini's corner cut and two side-square cuts — Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, p.166 ("fold twice, straight corner cut + two side squares removed...."). Students open and examine. The teacher asks: where are the holes, and how many sides does the opening have?

The teacher poses Challenge 1 — Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 1, p.166 ("predict where the hole and cut appear when Rani's paper is opened...."). Students first draw their prediction on paper, then fold and cut to verify. Pairs compare predictions with outcomes and articulate what the symmetry of folding does to a single cut.

Challenge 3 is posed — Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 3, p.166 ("fold twice; where to cut for a square hole in the centre...."). Students think independently, sketch the fold-cut plan, then execute and check. Groups share how many cuts they needed and where they placed them.

periods.teacher_notes: The fold-and-cut work builds directly on the mirror-line understanding developed through ink-blot and airplane folding — each fold creates a line of reflection, and a cut made on the folded paper appears symmetrically when opened. A frequent error is cutting too close to the fold edge, which removes the fold and produces an open strip rather than a hole; alert students to leave a margin from the folded edges. Challenge 2 (one fold, two mid-cuts, counting sides) is set as home practice.
materials: Square sheets of paper (several per student)

section_titles: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
periods.activity_title: Dot Grids, Mirrors, and Secret Writing

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, Symmetry in shapes Q1, p.167
tasks_in_class.description: Draw the border shapes (kite, arrow, envelope, triangle) on the dot grid; identify which are symmetrical; draw the lines of symmetry.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2a, p.168
tasks_in_class.description: Where should the mirror be placed on shape A to produce each of the six given shapes (1–6)?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Ambulance / mirror writing, p.169
tasks_in_class.description: Discuss why letters on an ambulance are written in reverse; identify mirror-written words (TAP, CAN, WOW, HEN); write words/names in mirror writing and challenge friends; try with your own language script.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 4. Complete symmetrical shapes, p.169
tasks_in_class.description: Complete the four half-shapes on the dot grid (two using a vertical axis, two using a horizontal axis) to make symmetrical figures.

time_bands.activity: Students open dot-grid pages and draw the four border shapes — Let Us Do, Symmetry in shapes Q1, p.167 ("draw kite, arrow, envelope, triangle; identify symmetrical; draw lines...."). After drawing, pairs share which shapes they found symmetrical and trace the line of symmetry with a coloured pencil.

Distribute small mirrors. Students work through the mirror-placement challenge — Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2a, p.168 ("where to place mirror on shape A for each of six shapes...."). For each derived shape, they record the mirror position (vertical, horizontal, diagonal) in a word or sketch.

The teacher holds up a picture of an ambulance and invites students to read the bonnet text — Let Us Do, 3. Ambulance / mirror writing, p.169 ("discuss why letters on ambulance are reversed; identify mirror words...."). Students then write their own name in mirror script and swap with a neighbour to decode.

Students complete the four half-shapes on the dot grid — Let Us Do, 4. Complete symmetrical shapes, p.169 ("complete four half-shapes using vertical and horizontal axes...."). The teacher circulates and asks one student to explain how they chose where to place each dot on the other side.

periods.teacher_notes: Tasks T-10, T-11, and T-12 (mirror numbers and the guess-my-number game) are closely related and address the same reasoning thread as T-9; they can be offered as additional practice — Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2b and Q2c, p.168 — to students who finish quickly or as a home exploration. A common error in completing half-shapes is reflecting the shape across the wrong axis; ask students to lay their ruler or a pencil along the axis line before plotting dots on the other side.
materials: Dot-grid paper or textbook dot-grid pages

section_titles: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
periods.activity_title: Tiles That Fit — Finding the Repeating Unit

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 5. Observe shapes, p.170
tasks_in_class.description: Observe the given shapes; count sides for each; count lines of symmetry for each; trace and fold to verify lines of symmetry.
Identify the repeating unit (tile) in each of the two given tile patterns and continue the patterns.
Which shapes have you used to make the tiles? Which of the tiles are symmetrical? Draw the lines of symmetry if any.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Tiles at the Tile Shop Q4, p.172
tasks_in_class.description: Look at the two rhombus/hexagon tessellation designs; discuss what you notice (shapes used, effect of colour, how colours create different visual patterns).

time_bands.activity: Students trace the shapes on p.170, count sides, and count lines of symmetry by folding — Let Us Do, 5. Observe shapes, p.170 ("count sides; count lines of symmetry; trace and fold to verify...."). Groups record their counts in a quick table on paper.

Students study the two tile-pattern grids and ring the repeating unit in pencil — Tiling the Tiles Q1, p.171 ("identify repeating unit in two tile patterns; continue patterns...."). They then continue each pattern for at least two more rows. Pairs compare where they placed the boundary of the repeating unit.

Students name the shapes composing each tile and mark lines of symmetry — Tiling the Tiles Q2, p.171 ("which shapes used; which tiles symmetrical; draw lines of symmetry...."). A few students share at the board, and the class decides whether the proposed line is genuine.

The teacher displays or points to the rhombus and hexagon tessellation designs on p.172 — Tiles at the Tile Shop Q4, p.172 ("observe two tessellations; discuss shapes, colour, visual patterns...."). A quick pair-share: what pattern do you see when only one colour is used, and what changes when two colours alternate?

periods.teacher_notes: The shapes observation (sides and symmetry) on p.170 connects the individual-shape symmetry work from the dot-grid and mirror tasks to the composite tile context that follows immediately. A common error is identifying only the largest visible shape as the repeating unit; encourage students to outline the smallest group of shapes that, when copied, fills the grid exactly.

section_titles: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
periods.activity_title: Design Your Tile, Build the Floor

tasks_in_class.description: Make more tiles by joining two or more shapes; trace them in your notebook to create paths with no gaps or overlaps.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Tiles at the Tile Shop, p.171
tasks_in_class.description: Design creative tiles of your own in the hexagonal and square spaces provided; use a rangometry kit or shape cutouts.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a catty wall, p.173
tasks_in_class.description: Take a square paper; mark cat ears/head outline; cut along outline; slide top piece down and tape; trace the cat tile to make a catty wall pattern with no gaps.

homework.book_ref: Let Us Do, 1. Make floor patterns, p.172
homework.description: Make a floor pattern with your tile (like Mini's triangle-diamond pattern); ensure no overlaps and no gaps.

time_bands.activity: Students join two or more shape cut-outs to form a new tile and trace it repeatedly in their notebooks — Tiling the Tiles Q3, p.171 ("join shapes; trace to create path with no gaps or overlaps...."). They check after every two traces that no gap has opened.

Using rangometry pieces or shape cut-outs, students fill the hexagonal and square grids with their own ornamental design — Tiles at the Tile Shop, p.171 ("design creative tiles in hexagonal and square spaces...."). The teacher circulates and asks: does your design have a line of symmetry?

Each student takes a fresh square of paper and follows the cat-tile steps — Let Us Do, 2. Making a catty wall, p.173 ("mark outline; cut; slide top piece; tape; trace catty wall with no gaps...."). They trace the tile at least six times to make a wall strip and observe that the irregular shape still tiles perfectly.

periods.teacher_notes: The cat-tile activity is an unhurried making activity that is the payoff for all the earlier tiling observation — students discover hands-on that a tile does not need to be a regular polygon to tessellate. A common error in making the cat tile is not sliding the cut piece far enough down before taping, which leaves the new shape unable to interlock; demonstrate the slide step explicitly before students begin.
materials: Square sheets of paper (several per student)
Shape cut-outs or rangometry kit pieces

section_titles: Nature walk — symmetry in the natural world
periods.activity_title: Nature Walk — Symmetry All Around Us

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174
tasks_in_class.description: Go on a nature walk; collect fallen leaves, petals, flowers; categorise as symmetrical/non-symmetrical; make designs and patterns; make a greeting card with leaf imprints; create animals or designs using leaves and flowers.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the nature walk purpose — Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174 ("collect fallen leaves, petals, flowers; observe symmetry in nature...."). Students are shown how to hold a leaf and fold it gently to test for symmetry. Each student takes a project sheet for recording observations.

Students walk to the school garden or courtyard and collect only fallen leaves, petals, and flowers — Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174. They sort collected items into two groups — symmetrical and non-symmetrical — and record at least three specimens from each group by outline-tracing or description on their project sheet.

Back in the classroom, students use their collected materials to make a greeting card with leaf imprints and then arrange leaves and flowers into an animal or pattern design — Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174 ("make designs; make greeting card with leaf imprints; create animals...."). Pairs share their card and explain which part of the design is symmetrical.

A gallery walk: students place their project sheets and cards on desks. The class does a quick circuit and leaves one sticky note or verbal comment on a neighbour's work noting one symmetrical feature they spotted. The teacher closes by asking: where in today's walk did symmetry surprise you most?

periods.teacher_notes: The nature walk anchors the chapter's concept of a line of symmetry in real objects students have touched and handled — connecting leaf shapes to the dot-grid and fold work practised earlier. A common error is declaring any roughly oval leaf symmetrical without checking; prompt students to fold the leaf or hold it to light to test whether both halves match.
materials: Project sheets or large chart paper (one per student)
Paint or ink pad (for leaf imprints)

items.section_title: Line of symmetry and mirror line
items.prompt: Priya folds a square sheet of paper exactly in half and presses paint near the fold. She opens the sheet and sees a design. Draw a simple shape that could appear on one half, and then show what the whole design looks like after she opens the paper. Mark the fold line on your drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student draws a shape (e.g. a blob or simple outline) on one side of a vertical line and its mirror image on the other side, with the fold line clearly marked in the middle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the paper and treat the fold as the line of symmetry — whatever appears on one side is reflected identically on the other side.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold and press paint to produce the design physically before drawing it. Stretch: ask them to draw a second design using a horizontal fold line.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 1. Ink Design, p.164
exercise.description: Fold a sheet of paper in half, sprinkle water-colour drops at the fold, press to spread colour, open and observe the symmetrical ink design produced.

items.section_title: Line of symmetry and mirror line
items.prompt: Rahul makes a paper airplane by folding a rectangular sheet in half along its length. After folding, the airplane has a line of symmetry. Where is that line of symmetry on the folded airplane?

options.label: A
options.text: Across the short width of the airplane wing

options.label: B
options.text: Along the fold edge where the two halves meet

options.label: C
options.text: Along the tip of the airplane nose

options.label: D
options.text: There is no line of symmetry on a folded airplane

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Along the fold edge where the two halves meet (option A).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The fold creates a mirror line — the crease is exactly the line of symmetry because both halves are identical reflections of each other.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks symmetry must run across the shorter dimension; they have not connected the fold to the mirror line.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student identifies a prominent feature (the nose) rather than the structural fold that makes both sides match.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not recognise that a symmetric fold produces a line of symmetry by definition.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold a sheet and place a mirror along the crease to see the reflection. Stretch: ask whether a single-fold airplane has more than one line of symmetry and how they would check.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (d)–(h), p.165
exercise.description: Fly the symmetrical plane; try making an asymmetrical plane; fly both and observe which flies longer; share observations with friends.

items.section_title: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
items.prompt: Sana folds a square sheet of paper in half once (left to right). She cuts a small triangle from the folded edge at the centre. Draw what the sheet looks like when she opens it. Mark the fold line and show where the cut-out appears.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When opened, there is a triangular notch on the left edge and a matching triangular notch on the right edge, both at the centre height, with the fold line running vertically down the middle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The fold creates a mirror line; a cut on the folded edge appears symmetrically on both sides when the paper is opened.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold and cut a real sheet, then trace the result before drawing. Stretch: ask what would happen if the cut were made on the open (non-folded) edge instead.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, p.166
exercise.description: Take a square sheet of paper; fold and cut to reproduce Mini's design (fold twice, straight corner cut + two side squares removed).

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: The word MOM is written on a card. When you hold a mirror vertically beside the letter M at the centre, the reflected image in the mirror looks like a word. What does the reflected image show?

options.label: A
options.text: MOM

options.label: B
options.text: MON

options.label: C
options.text: MQM

options.label: D
options.text: WOW

teacher_guide.expected_answer: MOM — the word reads the same in the mirror because the letters M, O, and M each have vertical symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A word whose letters each have the same vertical mirror image will read identically when a vertical mirror is placed beside it.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses vertical and horizontal mirror effects, picturing the word flipped upside down.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student does not recognise that M has vertical symmetry and substitutes a different letter.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student applies an incorrect letter-reflection rule, changing M to Q.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a physical mirror on the printed word to observe the reflection directly. Stretch: ask the student to find one more three-letter word whose mirror image is the same word.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Ambulance / mirror writing, p.169
exercise.description: Discuss why letters on an ambulance are written in reverse; identify mirror-written words (TAP, CAN, WOW, HEN); write words/names in mirror writing and challenge friends; try with your own language script.

items.section_title: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
items.prompt: Look at the cat-tile activity in your book. Rohan cuts a square piece of paper, slides the top cut piece to the bottom, and tapes it. He now has an irregular shape. When he traces this shape many times on a large sheet, does it leave any gaps? Explain why or why not in one or two sentences.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No gaps are left. The interlocking bumps and dents on opposite edges of the tile fit together perfectly because the cut piece that was removed from one side was added to the other side, so every bump on one tile fits into a matching dent on the next tile.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A slide-cut tile tessellates because material removed from one edge is added to the opposite edge, making the edges interlock without gaps.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically make the cat tile and trace it twice to observe the fit before writing. Stretch: ask whether the same slide-cut technique would work starting with a rectangle instead of a square.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a catty wall, p.173
exercise.description: Take a square paper; mark cat ears/head outline; cut along outline; slide top piece down and tape; trace the cat tile to make a catty wall pattern with no gaps.

items.section_title: Nature walk — symmetry in the natural world
items.prompt: During a nature walk, children collect four leaves. Which of the following descriptions best shows that a leaf is symmetrical?

options.label: A
options.text: The leaf has a bright green colour on both sides.

options.label: B
options.text: The leaf has more than five points around its edge.

options.label: C
options.text: The leaf is larger than the other leaves collected.

options.label: D
options.text: When the leaf is folded along its central vein, the two halves match exactly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When the leaf is folded along its central vein, the two halves match exactly (option A).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A leaf is symmetrical if the fold along its central vein produces two halves that are mirror images of each other.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses colour uniformity with symmetry; colour is unrelated to whether the shape has a line of symmetry.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student uses size as a criterion; symmetry is about matching halves, not about overall area.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student focuses on the count of points rather than whether the two sides mirror each other.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student hold a real leaf and fold it to check before answering. Stretch: ask the student to describe a leaf that would NOT be symmetrical and explain how they would test it.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Let us go on a nature walk, p.174
exercise.description: Go on a nature walk; collect fallen leaves, petals, flowers; categorise as symmetrical/non-symmetrical; make designs and patterns; make a greeting card with leaf imprints; create animals or designs using leaves and flowers.

items.section_title: Line of symmetry and mirror line
items.prompt: An airplane shape (like the one in your book) has one line of symmetry along its length. If you fold the airplane shape along that line of symmetry, what must be true about the two wing halves? Explain your thinking in one or two sentences.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two wing halves must be exactly the same size and shape and must fit perfectly on top of each other when folded along the line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The line of symmetry is the fold line; both halves are mirror images, so they overlap exactly when folded.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to fold a paper airplane and check before writing. Stretch: ask what would happen to the flight if one wing were made slightly larger — would the line of symmetry still hold?

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Making a paper airplane (a)–(c), p.165
exercise.description: Mark the line of symmetry in Fig. 3, 4, and 5; count how many lines of symmetry Fig. 8 has; decide where to place a mirror to see the right-half reflection and whether it matches the left half.

items.section_title: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
items.prompt: Tara folds a square sheet of paper once (top to bottom). She cuts a small square from the top-right corner of the folded paper. When she opens the sheet, where will the square cut-outs appear?

options.label: A
options.text: Four cut-outs, one at each corner

options.label: B
options.text: One cut-out at the top-right corner and one at the bottom-right corner

options.label: C
options.text: One cut-out at the top-right corner and one at the top-left corner

options.label: D
options.text: One cut-out only at the top-right corner

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One cut-out at the top-right corner and one at the bottom-right corner (option A).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Folding top to bottom makes the top-right and bottom-right corners lie on top of each other; cutting through both layers at the corner removes material from both positions when the sheet is opened.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student forgets that folding places two layers under the scissors, so only one cut-out results from cutting one layer.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student imagines a left-right fold instead of a top-bottom fold, misidentifying which corners are stacked.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks folding once stacks all four corners, confusing one fold with two folds.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold and cut a scrap piece of paper to observe before answering. Stretch: ask where the cut-outs would appear if the paper were folded twice before cutting the same corner.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 1, p.166
exercise.description: Predict where the hole and cut will appear when Rani's twice-folded paper (corner cut + two side squares) is opened.

items.section_title: Holes and Cuts — fold-and-cut spatial reasoning
items.prompt: Meera folds a square sheet twice (first left to right, then top to bottom). She wants to cut a square hole that appears exactly in the centre of the full sheet when opened. How many cuts does she need to make, and where on the folded paper should she cut? Explain in one or two sentences.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She needs to make one cut — a square cut at the corner of the folded paper that is the centre of the original sheet (the corner where both fold lines meet). When opened, this single cut produces a square hole in the centre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: After two folds the paper's centre becomes the inner corner; one square cut there appears as a centred hole in all four layers when unfolded.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fold and mark the corner with a pencil dot before cutting. Stretch: ask what shape hole would appear if a circular cut were made at the same corner.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 3. Holes and Cuts, Challenge 3, p.166
exercise.description: Fold a paper twice. Where would you cut to make a square hole in the centre? How many cuts are required?

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: A student draws a kite shape and an arrow shape on dot paper. She says: 'Both shapes have exactly one line of symmetry.' Is she correct?

options.label: A
options.text: No — a kite has two lines of symmetry and an arrow has none.

options.label: B
options.text: No — neither the kite nor the arrow has any line of symmetry.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — a kite has one vertical line of symmetry and an arrow has one horizontal line of symmetry.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — both shapes have two lines of symmetry each.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes — a kite has one vertical line of symmetry and an arrow has one line of symmetry (option A).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold each shape along the proposed line; if both halves match exactly, the fold line is a line of symmetry — each shape has exactly one such line.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses the kite's two pairs of equal sides with two lines of symmetry; only the diagonal joining the unequal vertices is a line of symmetry for a typical kite.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student applies a visual judgement without testing, dismissing both shapes as asymmetric.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student over-counts, perhaps imagining perpendicular bisectors for both shapes without folding to verify.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace and fold the shapes to check. Stretch: ask the student to draw one shape that has two lines of symmetry and explain how they verified both.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, Symmetry in shapes Q1, p.167
exercise.description: Draw the border shapes (kite, arrow, envelope, triangle) on the dot grid; identify which are symmetrical; draw the lines of symmetry.

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: A student places a mirror vertically on the right side of a shape that looks like the letter L. The mirror image combined with the original creates a new shape. Describe what the combined shape looks like and whether it has a line of symmetry.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The combined shape looks like a rectangular U or a square bracket pair — an L on the left and its mirror-image reverse-L on the right, joined at the vertical mirror line. The combined shape has one vertical line of symmetry along the mirror line.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Placing a vertical mirror beside a shape joins the original and its reflection; the mirror line becomes the line of symmetry of the combined figure.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a physical mirror beside a drawn L shape and trace the reflected image. Stretch: ask the student to predict what combined shape is formed if the mirror is placed horizontally below the L instead.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 2. Games with a Mirror Q2a, p.168
exercise.description: Where should the mirror be placed on shape A to produce each of the six given shapes (1–6)?

items.section_title: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
items.prompt: In a tile pattern, the repeating unit is a rectangle made of two equal right-angled triangles joined along their longest side. Does this repeating unit have a line of symmetry? If yes, how many lines of symmetry does it have, and where are they? Explain your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. The rectangle has two lines of symmetry — one running horizontally through its midpoints and one running vertically through its midpoints. (If the rectangle is actually a square, a third and fourth diagonal line of symmetry also exist, but for a non-square rectangle, exactly two lines of symmetry.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the rectangle along each proposed line; the two halves match for the horizontal midline and the vertical midline, giving two lines of symmetry.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace the shape and fold the tracing to test. Stretch: ask whether the two triangles that make up the rectangle each have their own lines of symmetry, and whether those match the rectangle's lines.

exercise.description: Identify the repeating unit (tile) in each of the two given tile patterns and continue the patterns.

items.section_title: Tiling the Tiles — tessellation and creative tile design
items.prompt: In a floor tile pattern made entirely of regular hexagons, a student claims that each hexagon has exactly two lines of symmetry. Is the student correct?

options.label: A
options.text: No — a regular hexagon has no lines of symmetry.

options.label: B
options.text: No — a regular hexagon has six lines of symmetry.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — a regular hexagon has exactly two lines of symmetry.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — a regular hexagon has two lines of symmetry, one horizontal and one vertical.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No — a regular hexagon has six lines of symmetry (option A).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace and fold a regular hexagon; three lines connect opposite vertices and three lines connect midpoints of opposite sides, each producing matching halves — six lines in total.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student applies the rectangle or diamond rule (two lines) to the hexagon without testing it by folding.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student incorrectly judges the hexagon as asymmetric, perhaps because it looks complex.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student recognises only the obvious horizontal and vertical fold lines and misses the four diagonal lines.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace a regular hexagon and fold it in different directions to count matching halves. Stretch: ask the student to predict how many lines of symmetry a regular pentagon would have.

exercise.description: Which shapes have you used to make the tiles? Which of the tiles are symmetrical? Draw the lines of symmetry if any.

items.section_title: Symmetry in shapes, mirror games, and mirror writing
items.prompt: On a dot grid, half of a shape is drawn to the left of a vertical axis line. The half-shape has dots at positions (0,0), (0,2), (2,2), and (2,0), forming a square on the left of the axis at x = 2. After completing the symmetrical figure by reflecting across the vertical axis, what are the dot positions of the right half?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (2,0), (2,2), (4,2), (4,0) — option A. The reflected square sits entirely to the right of x = 2, with its left edge on the axis.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reflect each point of the left half across the vertical axis at x = 2 by keeping the y-coordinate the same and computing the new x as 2 + (2 − x_original).

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student copies the original left-half points rather than reflecting them, placing the right half on top of the left half.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student duplicates the bottom-left point (2,0) instead of including (4,0), showing confusion about the reflection of the bottom-right corner.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student shifts the shape upward instead of reflecting it sideways across the vertical axis.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student place a ruler along the axis line and count dots across to the right to find each reflected point. Stretch: ask the student to reflect the same square across a horizontal axis and state the new dot positions.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do, 4. Complete symmetrical shapes, p.169
exercise.description: Complete the four half-shapes on the dot grid (two using a vertical axis, two using a horizontal axis) to make symmetrical figures.
